chapterTitle: Scaling Ansible with Collections, Dynamic Inventory, and Performance Tuning

screens.title: Scaling Ansible with Collections, Dynamic Inventory, and Performance Tuning
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn three linked capabilities that make Ansible work at scale. First, Collections package modules, plugins, roles and docs into versioned bundles so teams can share and consume automation in a predictable way. Second, dynamic inventory lets Ansible query a live source — a cloud A P I, CMDB, or a custom script — so hosts are discovered at runtime instead of maintained by hand. Third, a few configuration choices such as forks, pipelining, fact caching, strategies, and asynchronous execution dramatically change how fast playbooks run when you manage hundreds or thousands of hosts. Each idea solves a concrete pain point: Collections avoid name conflicts and dependency drift, dynamic inventory prevents stale host lists, and tuning reduces wasted time and control-node load. For example, using a cloud inventory plugin allows grouping hosts by tags so your playbook targets only production web servers automatically. A common misconception is that increasing forks alone solves all performance problems; in practice you trade control-node C P U and complexity, so you must tune several knobs together. As you move through these screens you'll see code examples, an inventory script, configuration fragments, and a full playbook that demonstrates how these pieces integrate. Keep the scenario in mind: automating web servers in a cloud environment with changing instances and a need for predictable, fast runs.

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: Collections, dynamic inventory, and tuning let you manage growing automation reliably and quickly. Together they prevent stale hosts, conflicting modules, and slow runs on large fleets.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Scaling Ansible
Scaling Ansible with Collections, Dynamic Inventory, and Performance Tuning
Make content modular, keep inventories current, and tune execution to run automation at fleet scale.
In this lesson

Learn to install and reference Collections, build a dynamic inventory for cloud resources, and apply forks, pipelining, fact caching, strategies, and async tasks to speed runs on many hosts.

Coming up

Practical examples include ansible-galaxy install, an aws_ec2 inventory config, a sample dynamic inventory script, ansible.cfg tuning, and a full playbook that combines these features.

Explore Key Topics
Collections
Package modules, roles, and plugins into versioned bundles to avoid conflicts and share content.
Dynamic Inventory
Query cloud APIs or scripts at runtime so hosts reflect the real environment.
Performance Tuning
Adjust forks, pipelining, facts, strategies, and async to run efficiently at scale.
Visual Concept
How the three capabilities relate
Collections
Dynamic Inventory
Performance Tuning
Collections provide the content; inventory supplies the hosts; tuning makes execution efficient. Together they scale automation reliably.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In these objectives you will see four measurable skills that prepare you to scale Ansible. First, understand the purpose of Collections: you should be able to explain why packaging modules, roles, plugins and docs together reduces conflicts and simplifies sharing. For example, a cloud provider publishing a collection avoids naming collisions and ensures consistent versions across teams. Second, install and use Collections: you will learn commands and how to reference modules by their fully qualified collection name so playbooks remain explicit and unambiguous. Third, implement dynamic inventory: you will be able to configure an inventory plugin or script to discover hosts at runtime, which prevents stale static inventories in cloud environments. As a concrete example, using an AWS EC2 plugin lets you group instances by tags automatically. Fourth, apply performance tuning: you will recognize and set parameters such as forks, pipelining, fact caching, and async tasks to reduce run time and control-node load. A common misconception is that one setting alone optimizes everything; instead, you will learn how to combine settings appropriately for your control node resources. Each objective maps to a competency milestone so you know when you can apply the skill in real deployments.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Bloom's Progression
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide maps the same four skills to a Bloom-style progression so you know how to practice them. Start with Learn: identify what a Collection contains and the command to install one. For example, installing community. general gives you many modules without copying individual files. Next, Understand: explain how the FQCN avoids module name conflicts and how an inventory plugin returns fresh host groups. A simple contrast: with static inventory you edit files manually; with dynamic inventory you query a source at runtime. Then Apply: install a collection, configure an aws_ec2 inventory file, and run a playbook against the returned host groups. Practically, set forks and pipelining in ansible. cfg to observe faster runs. Finally Master: combine collections, dynamic inventory, and performance settings into repeatable project configuration so your automation scales reliably. A common misconception is equating higher forks with universal improvement — mastery requires balancing forks with control-node resources, caching, and strategy choices. Use the milestones to validate that you can run, troubleshoot, and tune real playbooks in a cloud environment.

screens.title: Ansible Collections — What and Why
screens.narratorSegment: Ansible Collections are a standardized package format that groups modules, roles, plugins, playbooks, and documentation into a single, versioned unit. The main benefit is modularity: instead of copying modules or maintaining ad-hoc libraries, teams consume tested, versioned collections. That prevents name collisions where two sources provide a module with the same short name. A clear example is a cloud provider distributing its modules as a collection; installing that collection gives you a consistent set of modules and plugins that are designed to work together. Collections also simplify dependency management because requirements can be declared and resolved with ansible-galaxy tools. A common misconception is treating collections as only a convenience; in reality they are a key part of maintainable automation at scale because they enable reproducible playbooks across environments. To validate your understanding, ask whether a playbook refers to a module by its short name or by a fully qualified collection name; the FQCN makes origins explicit. When teams share automation, prefer collections so that upgrades and rollbacks are controlled by versions rather than by manual file distribution. In short, Collections reduce drift, clarify ownership, and make content distribution predictable.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Collections bundle Ansible content into versioned packages to improve modularity and avoid conflicts.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Collections — Definition
What is a Collection?

A versioned package that can contain modules, plugins, roles, playbooks, and docs — distributed and installed with ansible-galaxy.

Modularity
Versioning
Dependency control
Distribution
Common misconception
Collections are optional conveniences. In reality, relying on collections prevents conflicts and enforces versioned content sharing across teams.
Concrete example

A cloud vendor publishes an official collection containing modules and plugins for its services. Installing that collection ensures you reference supported modules with an expected API.

Key Takeaway
Use Collections to package and share curated Ansible content so playbooks remain explicit and stable.
Check your understanding: can you name a module you use and whether it should be referenced by its FQCN to avoid ambiguity?

screens.title: Installing and Using Collections
screens.narratorSegment: Installing a collection is a simple and repeatable step that makes its content available to your playbooks. Use ansible-galaxy collection install followed by the collection name to add content to your environment. For example, installing community. general provides many general-purpose modules and plugins. Once installed, the Fully Qualified Collection Name, or FQCN, lets you reference a module unambiguously, such as community. general. ini_file. This avoids collisions with any other ini_file implementation you may have. In practice, you can also list collections at the top of a playbook to allow short module names from those collections. A common mistake is assuming a short module name always resolves the same way; when two collections provide a short name, only the FQCN is safe. Try installing a collection and then running a small play that uses community. general. ini_file to modify a local file. Watch for version differences and pin collection versions in a requirements file if you need reproducibility. Finally, remember that collections include documentation and example usage, which helps teams adopt modules without guessing argument names. Installing and Using Collections means use ansible-galaxy collection install and reference modules with their fqcn to ensure clarity and avoid conflicts.. In practical terms, ansible-galaxy and the fqcn pattern. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Install and reference
keyIdea.text: Use ansible-galaxy collection install and reference modules with their FQCN to ensure clarity and avoid conflicts.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Installing Collections
Install command
ansible-galaxy collection install community.general
FQCN example
# In a playbook you can reference a module by FQCN
- name: Ensure an INI file section exists
  community.general.ini_file:
    path: /tmp/my_config.ini
    section: database
    option: host
    value: db.example.com
    state: present
Tip: Use collections: at the top of a play to allow short names for modules provided by listed collections.
Example playbook fragment
---
- name: Example playbook using an Ansible Collection
  hosts: localhost
  collections:
    - community.general
  tasks:
    - name: Ensure an INI file section exists
      community.general.ini_file:
        path: /tmp/my_config.ini
        section: database
        option: host
        value: db.example.com
        state: present
Key Takeaway

Install collections with ansible-galaxy and prefer FQCNs when you need explicit, conflict-free module references.

screens.title: FQCN vs short module names
screens.narratorSegment: When you write playbooks you have two ways to reference modules: the short name (for example ini_file) or the Fully Qualified Collection Name, like community. general. ini_file. The short form is concise and works when only one provider supplies that module name. However, as your automation uses more third-party content, multiple collections may offer modules with the same short name. The FQCN removes ambiguity by specifying the collection owner and module name together. A concrete example is using community. general. ini_file versus another collection’s ini_file: the short name could resolve to either depending on collection search order, causing surprising behavior. A common misconception is that collections only add verbosity; the trade-off is explicit origin, which improves maintainability and debugging. If you list collections: at the top of a playbook you can often use shorter module names for those collections, but explicit FQCN usage is the safest choice for shared repositories. Practice: run a playbook using a module with both the short name and the FQCN and observe which module implementation was used. Your takeaway should be to prefer FQCNs when sharing or when multiple providers might exist.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › FQCN vs Short Name
Short name example
- name: Modify INI (short name)
  ini_file:
    path: /tmp/my_config.ini
    section: database
    option: host
    value: db.example.com
Concise but ambiguous if multiple collections provide ini_file.
FQCN example
- name: Modify INI (FQCN)
  community.general.ini_file:
    path: /tmp/my_config.ini
    section: database
    option: host
    value: db.example.com
Explicit and safe for shared or mixed-content repositories.
Key Takeaway

Prefer FQCN for reproducibility and clarity, especially when sharing playbooks or using multiple collections.

screens.title: Dynamic Inventory — Why it matters
screens.narratorSegment: Dynamic inventory solves the problem of stale host lists in environments where instances are created and destroyed frequently. Unlike a static inventory file, dynamic inventory queries an external source at runtime — for example a cloud A P I, a CMDB, or a custom script — and returns the current hosts and variables. This real-time discovery prevents playbooks from targeting hosts that no longer exist and enables grouping based on real attributes like tags. A practical example is using an AWS EC2 inventory plugin with filters for environment tags so only production, running instances are returned. One common misconception is that dynamic inventory is only for very large fleets; in fact, it is beneficial anytime instances are ephemeral or when metadata-driven grouping reduces manual inventory maintenance. For testing, you can create a simple inventory script that emits JSON; Ansible will accept that output as inventory. When adopting dynamic inventory, be mindful of A P I rate limits and authentication. The key benefit is a single source of truth: your cloud provider or CMDB becomes the authoritative inventory and Ansible reads it at runtime, keeping automation aligned with reality.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Dynamic inventory queries an external source at runtime, ensuring Ansible targets the current set of hosts and variables.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Dynamic Inventory — Definition
Why use dynamic inventory?
  • Automatically discover hosts that are running now.
  • Group hosts by tags, roles, or other metadata.
  • Avoid manual edits and stale data in cloud environments.
Concrete example

Use an aws_ec2 inventory plugin to filter instances by tag Environment: production and instance-state-name: running so only production hosts are returned at runtime.

Key Takeaway

Prefer dynamic inventory in cloud or ephemeral environments so your playbooks always target the right hosts and groups.

screens.title: AWS EC2 Inventory Plugin Example
screens.narratorSegment: Inventory plugins let Ansible talk to cloud providers using a small configuration file. The aws_ec2 inventory file declares the plugin, the regions to query, filters to select instances, and keyed_groups to create groups from tags. For example, setting regions to us-east-1, filters to tag:Environment: production and instance-state-name: running returns only active production instances. The keyed_groups feature automatically creates inventory groups based on tags like Name and Role, producing group names such as tag_Name_web01 or tag_Role_webserver. This makes targeting easier: your playbook can select hosts by tag-based groups instead of IP addresses. A typical workflow is to save this YAML as aws_ec2. yml and run ansible-playbook -i aws_ec2. yml my_playbook. yml. A common error is forgetting credentials or region configuration so the plugin returns no hosts; ensure your environment has suitable AWS credentials or an appropriate profile. Also be mindful of A P I rate limits when querying very large accounts. Dynamic grouping reduces maintenance and keeps an up-to-date mapping from cloud metadata to Ansible groups. AWS EC2 Inventory Plugin Example means use an inventory plugin file to query cloud apis and return up-to-date host lists grouped by metadata.. In practical terms, configure an inventory file to return instances by region, state and tags. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Inventory plugin
keyIdea.text: Use an inventory plugin file to query cloud APIs and return up-to-date host lists grouped by metadata.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › AWS EC2 Inventory Plugin
aws_ec2.yml
# aws_ec2.yml
plugin: amazon.aws.aws_ec2
regions:
  - us-east-1
filters:
  tag:Environment: production
  instance-state-name: running
keyed_groups:
  - key: tags.Name
    prefix: tag_Name_
  - key: tags.Role
    prefix: tag_Role_
Save as aws_ec2.yml and reference with ansible-playbook -i aws_ec2.yml.
Practical notes
  • Ensure AWS credentials or an instance profile are available.
  • Filters limit returned instances and reduce API calls.
  • Keyed groups create human-friendly group names from tags.
Key Takeaway

An inventory plugin configuration file queries the provider and returns groups you can target directly, avoiding manual host lists.

screens.title: Custom Dynamic Inventory Script
screens.narratorSegment: When an inventory plugin is not available, you can provide a custom inventory script that prints JSON in the format Ansible expects. The chapter includes a lightweight Python example that demonstrates the mechanism: it prints a JSON object with groups, hosts, group variables, and _meta hostvars. This example returns a webservers group with localhost as a host and provides variables like http_port and max_connections. The point of such a script is not the static data but the pattern: replace the hard-coded content with A P I calls to your cloud provider or CMDB, and format the returned data the same way. A common mistake is forgetting to make the script executable; remember to chmod +x dynamic_inventory dot P Y file. Also test the script independently by running it to verify valid JSON output. Using a script during development helps you iterate quickly before switching to an inventory plugin. In production, prefer plugins when available for better maintenance and performance, but custom scripts remain a practical fallback for custom sources. In practical terms, a simple json-producing script as a placeholder for cloud queries. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: A script that prints inventory JSON demonstrates the dynamic mechanism and can be adapted to query any external source.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Custom Inventory Script
dynamic_inventory.py
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import json
print(json.dumps({
    "webservers": {
        "hosts": ["localhost"],
        "vars": {
            "http_port": 80,
            "max_connections": 200
        }
    },
    "_meta": {
        "hostvars": {
            "localhost": {
                "ansible_connection": "local"
            }
        }
    }
}))
Make executable with chmod +x dynamic_inventory.py and reference it as your inventory.
Practical guidance
  • Run the script directly to confirm valid JSON.
  • Replace static data with API calls to return live host lists.
  • Ensure authentication and error handling for production scripts.
Key Takeaway

Custom inventory scripts demonstrate dynamic inventory behavior and can be adapted to any external data source for runtime discovery.

screens.title: Performance Tuning — Key Parameters
screens.narratorSegment: Performance tuning focuses on a few configuration knobs that have outsized impact when you manage many hosts. The forks parameter controls how many parallel processes Ansible uses; increasing forks lets more hosts be handled concurrently but consumes control-node C P U and memory. Start with moderate increases and observe resource usage. Pipelining reduces SSH round-trips by sending multiple module operations over one connection; enabling pipelining often yields large gains over high-latency networks. Fact caching stores previously gathered facts in a cache such as a JSON file or Redis so you avoid re-gathering unchanged facts every run; this saves time when facts rarely change. A typical mistake is leaving gather_facts enabled when facts aren't needed — setting gather_facts: false at the play level when possible can dramatically reduce runtime. Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Performance Tuning — Parameters
forks
Controls parallel processes. Increase to run tasks on more hosts simultaneously, but monitor control-node CPU and RAM.
pipelining
Reduces SSH round-trips by sending multiple module operations over a single connection. Useful on high-latency networks.
fact_caching
Store gathered facts in a cache so subsequent runs avoid re-collecting unchanged data. Choose jsonfile, redis, or another supported cache backend.
strategy
linear waits for batches; free lets hosts proceed independently. Use free when task duration varies but accept debugging complexity.
Key Takeaway

Combine settings: increase forks cautiously, enable pipelining, cache facts when they are stable, and choose a strategy that matches your task profile.

screens.title: Gathering Facts and Fact Caching
screens.narratorSegment: Fact gathering collects system details from hosts at the start of a play. While often useful, gathering facts on every run can be costly at scale. If your playbook does not depend on facts, set gather_facts: false to skip the step and save time. screens.title: Asynchronous Tasks and Long-Running Work
screens.narratorSegment: Long-running operations can block the control node if handled synchronously. Ansible's async and poll keywords let you start a task on a host and check its status later, freeing the control node to manage other hosts. In the example play, a shell task starts a long-running script with async: 3600 and poll: 10, allowing the task to run up to an hour while checking status periodically. You capture the job id in a register and then use async_status with the job id to poll for completion, typically inside an until loop. A common misconception is that async removes the need to monitor the task; you still should follow up to ensure completion. Also note that using async increases the need for careful error handling and retries. Practical use cases include installing large packages, database migrations, or long deployments where you do not want every host to remain locked waiting for one long step. Use async when long waits would otherwise stall many hosts and when you can tolerate eventual consistency across the fleet. In practical terms, use async and poll to start, track, and free the control node. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Async Tasks
Async example
---
- name: Demonstrate performance tuning with async tasks
  hosts: webservers
  tasks:
    - name: Start a very long-running process asynchronously
      ansible.builtin.shell: /opt/long_running_script.sh
      async: 3600
      poll: 10
      register: long_task_result

    - name: Wait for the long-running process to complete (if poll was 0)
      ansible.builtin.async_status:
        jid: "{{ long_task_result.ansible_job_id }}"
      register: async_status_result
      until: async_status_result.finished
      retries: 360
      delay: 10
      when: long_task_result.ansible_job_id is defined and long_task_result.poll == 0
Remember: async frees the control node, but you must track job ids and handle retries and failures appropriately.
Common mistake
Assuming async guarantees success. You must check status and design retry logic for robust orchestration.

That question directs practical next steps.

In this chapter you will learn three linked capabilities that make Ansible work at scale. First, Collections package modules, plugins, roles and docs into versioned bundles so teams can share and consume automation in a predictable way. Second, dynamic inventory lets Ansible query a live source — a cloud A P I, CMDB, or a custom script — so hosts are discovered at runtime instead of maintained by hand. Third, a few configuration choices such as forks, pipelining, fact caching, strategies, and asynchronous execution dramatically change how fast playbooks run when you manage hundreds or thousands of hosts. Each idea solves a concrete pain point: Collections avoid name conflicts and dependency drift, dynamic inventory prevents stale host lists, and tuning reduces wasted time and control-node load. For example, using a cloud inventory plugin allows grouping hosts by tags so your playbook targets only production web servers automatically. A common misconception is that increasing forks alone solves all performance problems; in practice you trade control-node C P U and complexity, so you must tune several knobs together. As you move through these screens you'll see code examples, an inventory script, configuration fragments, and a full playbook that demonstrates how these pieces integrate. Keep the scenario in mind: automating web servers in a cloud environment with changing instances and a need for predictable, fast runs.

In these objectives you will see four measurable skills that prepare you to scale Ansible. First, understand the purpose of Collections: you should be able to explain why packaging modules, roles, plugins and docs together reduces conflicts and simplifies sharing. For example, a cloud provider publishing a collection avoids naming collisions and ensures consistent versions across teams. Second, install and use Collections: you will learn commands and how to reference modules by their fully qualified collection name so playbooks remain explicit and unambiguous. Third, implement dynamic inventory: you will be able to configure an inventory plugin or script to discover hosts at runtime, which prevents stale static inventories in cloud environments. As a concrete example, using an AWS EC2 plugin lets you group instances by tags automatically. Fourth, apply performance tuning: you will recognize and set parameters such as forks, pipelining, fact caching, and async tasks to reduce run time and control-node load. A common misconception is that one setting alone optimizes everything; instead, you will learn how to combine settings appropriately for your control node resources. Each objective maps to a competency milestone so you know when you can apply the skill in real deployments.

This second objectives slide maps the same four skills to a Bloom-style progression so you know how to practice them. Start with Learn: identify what a Collection contains and the command to install one. For example, installing community. general gives you many modules without copying individual files. Next, Understand: explain how the FQCN avoids module name conflicts and how an inventory plugin returns fresh host groups. A simple contrast: with static inventory you edit files manually; with dynamic inventory you query a source at runtime. Then Apply: install a collection, configure an aws_ec2 inventory file, and run a playbook against the returned host groups. Practically, set forks and pipelining in ansible. cfg to observe faster runs. Finally Master: combine collections, dynamic inventory, and performance settings into repeatable project configuration so your automation scales reliably. Ansible Collections are a standardized package format that groups modules, roles, plugins, playbooks, and documentation into a single, versioned unit. The main benefit is modularity: instead of copying modules or maintaining ad-hoc libraries, teams consume tested, versioned collections. That prevents name collisions where two sources provide a module with the same short name. A clear example is a cloud provider distributing its modules as a collection; installing that collection gives you a consistent set of modules and plugins that are designed to work together. Collections also simplify dependency management because requirements can be declared and resolved with ansible-galaxy tools. A common misconception is treating collections as only a convenience; in reality they are a key part of maintainable automation at scale because they enable reproducible playbooks across environments. To validate your understanding, ask whether a playbook refers to a module by its short name or by a fully qualified collection name; the FQCN makes origins explicit. When teams share automation, prefer collections so that upgrades and rollbacks are controlled by versions rather than by manual file distribution. In short, Collections reduce drift, clarify ownership, and make content distribution predictable.

Installing a collection is a simple and repeatable step that makes its content available to your playbooks. Long-running operations can block the control node if handled synchronously. Ansible's async and poll keywords let you start a task on a host and check its status later, freeing the control node to manage other hosts. In the example play, a shell task starts a long-running script with async: 3600 and poll: 10, allowing the task to run up to an hour while checking status periodically. You capture the job id in a register and then use async_status with the job id to poll for completion, typically inside an until loop. A common misconception is that async removes the need to monitor the task; you still should follow up to ensure completion. Also note that using async increases the need for careful error handling and retries. Practical use cases include installing large packages, database migrations, or long deployments where you do not want every host to remain locked waiting for one long step. Use async when long waits would otherwise stall many hosts and when you can tolerate eventual consistency across the fleet. Summarizing the most important ideas helps you retain them. First, Ansible Collections bundle modules, roles, and plugins into versioned packages; use ansible-galaxy to install them and prefer FQCNs to avoid ambiguity. Second, Dynamic Inventory provides a runtime view of hosts by querying external sources such as cloud APIs or custom scripts; this prevents stale inventories and enables tag-based grouping. Third, Performance Tuning matters: adjust forks, enable pipelining, cache facts when appropriate, control gather_facts, use suitable strategy plugins, and leverage async for long-running tasks. Each of these three areas addresses a specific scaling pain point: content drift, stale host lists, and slow execution. A healthy approach is to treat them together: use collections to standardize modules, dynamic inventory to get the right targets, and tuning to make your runs efficient. Ask yourself which of these three you should adopt first based on your current pain: are your modules inconsistent, do your hosts change frequently, or are playbooks too slow? That question directs practical next steps.

Use this checklist before you run automation at scale. First, install and reference Collections so modules are explicit and versioned. Confirm the collection provides the module you expect and use FQCNs when in doubt. Second, validate your dynamic inventory by running the inventory plugin or script and inspecting returned groups; ensure credentials and filters are correct so you target the expected hosts. Third, review performance settings: set forks based on control-node capacity, enable pipelining for high-latency links, disable or cache facts as appropriate, and consider async for long-running operations. A useful habit is to run small, instrumented test runs after each change to measure the effect. These three reminders map directly to the chapter: package content, discover hosts at runtime, and tune execution — do them together and you will avoid the common pitfalls of scale.
